catalog_quote: Stress in Panyjima operates as follows: 1.Primary stress falls on the first long vowel in the word. If there is no long vowel, primary stress falls on the first syllable in the word. 2. If there is a non-initial long vowel occurring in the word, secondary stress will fall on the first syllable. If primary stress falls on the first syllable then secondary stress will fall on either the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable depending on the morphological structure of the word. The placement of primary and secondary stress on words not having non-initial long vowels can be approximated by the follwing rules. Firstly, stress is assigned to the syllables in the word according to the morphological structure of the word. ... Rule a. states that the first syllable in a word or non-monosyllabic morpheme will be stressed. Rule b. states that where there is a sequence of three unstressed syllables, the middle syllable receives stress. Secondly, primary stress is assigned to the first stressed syllable in the word, and secondary stress to the last stressed syllable in the word. All other stressed syllables retain some slight emphasis which might be called rhythmic stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes to the leftmost long vowel in the word (unbounded, quantity-sensitive); in words with no long vowel (the great majority, since long vowels are rare) primary stress is word-initial. Non-primary stresses are assigned morphologically: the first syllable of the word and of every polysyllabic morpheme is stressed, and in any run of three unstressed syllables the middle one is stressed; the first stressed syllable gets primary stress, the last stressed syllable secondary stress, the rest 'rhythmic stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 18: if a non-initial long vowel carries primary stress, secondary stress falls on the first syllable; otherwise secondary stress falls on the last stressed syllable (penult or antepenult depending on morphological structure), with the first syllable of each non-monosyllabic morpheme stressed and 'all other stressed syllables retain some slight emphasis which might be called rhythmic stress'. Goedemans 1998 Appendix D codes it (M)(Ed)(RS): morphology plays a role, secondary at the edge opposite main stress, regular secondary stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 20: 'There are a number of exceptions to these rules of stress placement. The exceptions all involve the verbal derivational affix -ma-' (e.g. mírli-mà-larta), analysed as -ma- being inherently stressed plus a rule erasing stress on a following suffix such as -larta; p. 21-22: 'At present there is not enough data to allow a formulation of the stress associated with the three words with non-initial long vowels', but the passive-participle (long-vowel) stress is describable; -ma- 'will not attract stress from long vowels'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word including suffixes); rules are stated over morphological structure of the word; no phrase-level statement. Not contrastive. Based on the author's own 1979-81 Onslow fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: Dench 1981 describes Panyjima as spoken at Onslow (Pilbara) by c. 60 speakers in 1979-81; no dialect split is made. Same glottocode pany1241 (ISO pnw). Thieberger 1993 and Bilybara 1992 note Palyku is sometimes treated as a dialect of Banyjima but Dench separates it; the stress statement concerns Panyjima proper.

sources.note: For Panyjima specifically the work is silent: the §4.4.1 entry has no phonology or stress section. The only stress sentence in the book is the generic 'usually on the first syllable' in the pronunciation guide (p. 6), which is compatible with the catalog's Dench 1981 rule (first long vowel, else first syllable — i.e. initial stress in the default case) but says nothing about long-vowel attraction or secondary stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the weight-sensitive reading.
